title: André Neher
content:
The Dialectics of Word and Silence: The Intellectual and Spiritual Legacy of André Neher
The intellectual history of the twentieth century witnessed a profound revaluation of religious identity in the shadow of total war and genocide, particularly within the Francophone Jewish world. André Neher, born Asher Dov Neher, stands as a central architect of this renewal, serving as a bridge between the traditional scholarship of Alsatian Judaism and the existentialist rigors of post-war European philosophy.[1, 2] His life and work represent a persistent attempt to navigate the "middle" or "diagonal" space between seemingly irreconcilable opposites: the sacred and the profane, the word and silence, and the historical reality of Auschwitz versus the eternal promise of Jerusalem.[3, 4] Neher’s contribution was not merely academic but communal; he was the "reviver of dry bones" for a French Jewish community that had seen its emancipationist ideals shattered by the collaboration of the Vichy regime and the machinery of the Holocaust.[1] By integrating biblical philology with metaphysical inquiry, Neher developed a "Prophetic Humanism" that placed the individual in a state of active, dialectical engagement with the Divine, even and especially when the Divine appeared to be silent.[5, 6]
Biographical Genesis: From Alsace to Mahanaim
The foundations of Neher's thought are inseparable from his roots in Alsace, a borderland region between French and German cultures. Born in 1914 in Obernai, Bas-Rhin, Neher was raised in an environment where the traditionalism of the German-Jewish "Neo-Orthodoxy" met the intellectual openness of French culture.[1, 2, 7] His early academic interests were focused on German literature, a pursuit that would later inform his literary approach to biblical texts.[2, 8] However, the onset of the Second World War and the rise of Nazism forced a radical shift. In 1940, following the implementation of anti-Jewish laws by the Vichy government, Neher was dismissed from his teaching position at the University of Strasbourg.[1, 2]
This exclusion from the academic world precipitated a period of internal exile. Neher, along with his father Albert and his brother Richard, fled to the village of Lanteuil in southern France.[1, 7] In a symbolic act of resistance and spiritual resilience, the family named their refuge "Mahanaim," a reference to the "Two Camps" established by the patriarch Jacob.[1] During these years of hiding, Neher dedicated himself to the intensive study of Jewish sources, particularly the Bible and the works of the Maharal of Prague, which provided the metaphysical scaffolding for his later writings.[4, 7] The ritual of hand-writing a "Haggadah of Mahanaim" each year during the war served as a psychological and spiritual anchor, reinforcing the belief that the Jewish people would once again be "in Jerusalem".[1]
The Strasbourg School and the Academic Institutionalization of Jewish Studies
In the immediate aftermath of the war, Neher became the driving force behind the intellectual reconstruction of French Jewry. In 1948, he was appointed to the newly created chair of Jewish Studies at the University of Strasbourg.[7, 9] This was a landmark event, as it represented the first formal recognition of "Ancient and Modern Jewish Literature" within the French university system.[9] Under his leadership, the "Strasbourg School" became a magnet for young Jewish intellectuals, particularly those from North Africa who arrived in the 1950s and 60s following decolonization.[7, 12]
Neher’s pedagogical approach was characterized by a rejection of the "cold" or "alienated" methods of nineteenth-century scholarship, such as the Wissenschaft des Judentums.[1, 3] Instead, he promoted a synthesis of academic rigor and personal engagement, arguing that the study of Jewish texts should be a transformative, existential experience.[3] He and his wife, Renée, were noted for their hospitality and their commitment to integrating Algerian Jews into the European Jewish fabric, fostering a sense of shared responsibility and Zionist aspiration.[7, 12] This period also saw Neher engage in pioneering interfaith dialogue, convincing Catholic and Protestant leaders of the legitimacy of Jewish national aspirations and the State of Israel.[7]
The Paris School and the Colloque des Intellectuels Juifs
Neher was a central figure in the Colloque des intellectuels juifs de langue française, a movement that redefined Jewish identity in post-war France.[11, 12] Alongside the philosopher Emmanuel Levinas and the educator Yehuda Leon Ashkenazi (Manitou), Neher formed an intellectual triumvirate that sought to reconcile traditional Jewish learning with the demands of modern French culture.[3, 11]
The Division of Intellectual Labor
Within the context of the Colloque, which held its first session in 1957, each leader specialized in a specific area of Jewish knowledge to address the existential crisis of a community that felt "lost" after the Holocaust.[3, 11, 12]
Emmanuel Levinas: Focused on the Talmud as a source for ethics and the philosophy of the "Other".[3, 14]
Yehuda Leon Ashkenazi (Manitou): Explored the Kabbalah and the secrets of the oral tradition to provide a redemptive historical framework.[3, 11]
André Neher: Concentrated on the Bible (Tanakh), using prophetic literature to construct a "Prophetic Humanism" that could respond to the dehumanization of modern mass society.[3, 5]
This collaboration was not merely academic; it was an attempt to forge a new "Jewish Consciousness" (La Conscience juive) that was no longer subservient to Western universalism but offered a distinct, particularist challenge to it.[11, 14, 15] Neher's work within this group emphasized the "Biblical Vocation" as a call to historical responsibility, arguing that the Jew must act as a witness to the Divine Word in the midst of a fractured world.[2, 12]
Prophetic Existence: The Metaphysics of Human Vocation
Neher’s work on prophecy, most notably in L’Essence du prophétisme (1955), represents a departure from traditional theological categories. He viewed the prophet not as a predictor of the future, but as an existential type defined by an "I-Thou" relationship with God.[6, 16] This relationship is characterized by a "diagonal" tension where the initiative is entirely Divine, yet the response must be authentically human.[4, 6]
The Biblical Concept of Navi
Neher analyzed the Hebrew word for prophet, Navi, as originating from the root meaning "to bubble forth" or "to fountain".[16, 17] This etymological insight was crucial to his understanding of the prophetic mission as a creative, linguistic event. The prophet is one through whom the Word overflows into the world, transforming the raw data of history into a meaningful, ethical narrative.[16] This "bubbling forth" is not a controlled intellectual process but an overwhelming, sometimes painful, encounter with the Divine that forces the individual out of their private solitude and into the public square.[17, 18]
Prophetic Humanism vs. Dehumanized Massification
A recurrent theme in Neher's thought is the critique of "massification"—the process by which modern society turns individuals into interchangeable cogs in a technical machine.[5] He argued that this dehumanization was the necessary precursor to Auschwitz.[5] In his study of Amos and Moses, Neher showed that the biblical prophets stood in opposition to similar forces of their own time: the "technical sadism" and "genocidal techniques" of Egypt, and the social exploitation of the northern kingdom of Israel.[5]
The Dialectic of Silence: L'Exיל de la Parole
Neher’s most profound philosophical contribution is his investigation into silence, detailed in his 1970 work L'Exil de la parole (The Exile of the Word).[2, 5] This work was a direct response to the silence of God during the Holocaust, a topic that many other theologians avoided or addressed only with standard apologies.[5, 22] For Neher, silence is not the absence of communication but a profound and structural form of the Divine Word itself.[2, 22]
Three Modalities of Biblical Silence
Neher identified several forms of silence in the Bible, each with its own metaphysical weight:
Cosmic Silence: The silence of the universe that precedes or accompanies creation. It represents the "void" or "night" from which the world is called into being.[5, 22] This silence is often expressed in the Psalms, where "there is no speech, there are no words," yet the message of the cosmos reaches the ends of the earth.[22]
Divine Silence as a Test: The silence of God in response to human suffering or prayer. Neher analyzes the Binding of Isaac (the Akedah) and the Book of Job as archetypal tests of silence.[5, 22] Abraham walks in a "blind, deaf, and mute" state, trusting in the Divine even when the Voice has ceased.[22] Job’s cries fall on "barred doors," yet it is precisely through this silence that he moves from a conventional religion to a genuine encounter with the Divine.[22]
Inertia vs. Energy: Neher distinguishes between "silence as inertia"—the despairing silence of Saul that leads to sorcery and suicide—and "silence as energy"—the potent, waiting silence of the prophets that stores up the Word for its eventual eruption.[5]
Auschwitz and the Ontological Suspension Bridge
Neher argued that "The silence is with Auschwitz".[5] He refused to offer simple answers for the tragedy, instead suggesting that the silence of God in the camps was a re-emergence of the "original void" that precedes creation.[5] This silence creates a state of "ontological insecurity," which Neher compared to a "suspension bridge" over an abyss.[2] To be human is to live on this bridge, facing the "radical factor of uncertainty" that silence imposes.[2] However, this silence is also the precondition for human freedom. If God spoke directly and constantly, human choice would be annihilated by the sheer force of Divine presence.[2]
The Maharal of Prague and the Dialectical Middle
Neher’s study of the Maharal of Prague, Le Puits de l'Exil (1962), was instrumental in reviving the reputation of Rabbi Judah Loew ben Bezalel as a modern philosopher.[4, 23] Neher saw in the Maharal a thinker who had anticipated the crises of modernity and offered a "dialectical theology" that could resolve the contradictions of Jewish existence.[4]
The Concept of the Middle
The Maharal’s philosophy, as interpreted by Neher, is built on the concept of the "middle" or the "interstitial space." He described this through three axes:
The Horizontal Axis: Represents the relationship between humans, governed by ethics and the quest for autonomy.[4, 24]
The Vertical Axis: Represents the relationship between man and the Creator, governed by a relative and limited epistemology.[4, 24]
The Diagonal Axis: The "Middle" that completes the other two. It is the site where contradictions are unified not by compromise, but by a higher synthesis.[4, 23]
Neher used this framework to explain the "adventure of truth" in Judaism—a journey that requires living "over the abyss of duality" without falling into the trap of binary thinking.[4] The Golem of Prague served as a warning about the limits of human creative power when divorced from this dialectical balance.[4]
The Renaissance of Hebrew and the Invention of the Profane
One of Neher’s most controversial and insightful theories concerned the nature of the "secular" in Judaism. In Le Conflit du sacré et du profane dans la renaissance de l'hébreu (1958), he argued that while most religions are based on the "sacred," Judaism is unique because it "invented the profane".[1, 2]
The Secularization of Authority
Neher posited that Judaism moved authority away from the "sacred" figures of priests and sorcerers and toward the "secular" or rational figures of the Rabbi, the Judge, and the Sage.[1] This was an "essential transfer" from charismatic, irrational power to a rational, legal framework.[1] He saw the rebirth of the Hebrew language in the State of Israel as the ultimate expression of this tension. For Neher, modern Hebrew is not merely a secular language; it is a "Holy Tongue" that has been purposefully "profaned" to allow for national life, yet it retains a "sacred residue" that constantly challenges the secular Israeli to remember their Divine vocation.[2]
Contrast with Other Thinkers
Neher’s position on the secular was distinct from his contemporaries:
Rav Kook: Sought to "sanctify the profane," seeing the secular as a hidden form of the holy.
Rav Soloveitchik: Granted the profane an "ideal" (l'chatchila) status but maintained clear boundaries.[1]
André Neher: Viewed the tension as a permanent, dialectical necessity. He did not want to "cure" the conflict between sacred and profane but to inhabit it as a source of creative energy.[1]
Aliyah and the Israeli Intellectual Environment
In 1974, at the age of sixty, Neher and his wife Renée fulfilled their lifelong goal of Aliyah, settling in the Rehavia neighborhood of Jerusalem.[1, 2, 13] He described his move to Israel as a "marriage" to the land, performed "by way of canopy and sanctification".[1] However, his arrival in Israel was marked by a significant intellectual and institutional disappointment.
The Rejection by the Hebrew University
The Israeli academic establishment, centered at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, largely ignored or rejected Neher’s work.[1, 3] The "Jerusalem School" of Jewish Studies was deeply committed to the Wissenschaft des Judentums model—objective, philological, and often detached.[3] Neher’s writing style, the Essai, was viewed as too personal, too literary, and lacking the rigorous footnote culture of "scientific" research.[3]
He was criticized for his interpretation of Amos, with scholars claiming he solved textual problems with "metaphysical and ideological assumptions" rather than objective evidence.[3] Similarly, his work on David Gans and the scientific revolution was dismissed by some for being too rooted in a "traditional-Jewish consciousness".[3, 25] Despite this, Neher found a welcoming environment at Tel Aviv University and the Van Leer Jerusalem Institute, where he continued to teach and influence a new generation of Israeli and Francophone students.[1, 7, 26]
Comparative Philosophy: Neher, Heschel, and Buber
Neher is often described as the "French Martin Buber" or a disciple of Abraham Joshua Heschel, though his philosophy had its own unique Alsatian and French character.[3, 21]
Neher and Heschel
Neher felt a profound connection to Heschel’s works, particularly Man is Not Alone and God in Search of Man.[21] He read them while in the Swiss Alps and was struck by Heschel’s rejection of the "legalistic" reduction of Judaism.[21, 28] Both thinkers shared a "pathos-driven" view of the Divine, where God is not a remote architect but a "searcher" for humanity.[21] They both emphasized the "wonder" and "spirit" of the biblical text over the dry analysis of the academy.[28, 29] However, where Heschel focused on the "divine pathos," Neher focused on the "divine silence," providing a darker, perhaps more existentialist, reading of the post-Holocaust condition.[21, 22]
Neher and Buber
Like Buber, Neher was interested in the "I-Thou" relationship, but Neher’s "Thou" was more deeply embedded in the specific philology and history of the Hebrew Bible.[3, 6] Neher also lacked Buber’s occasional anarchic attitude toward Halakha (Jewish Law). For Neher, the Law was the "secular" structure that protected the "sacred" word, and he remained more traditionally observant than Buber.[1]
The Historiographical Contribution of Renée Neher-Bernheim
It is impossible to discuss Neher’s work without mentioning his wife and constant collaborator, Renée Neher-Bernheim.[7] A prominent historian in her own right, she provided the historical grounding for many of Neher's metaphysical explorations. Her works, such as Le Judaïsme dans le monde romain and her multi-volume history of the Jewish people from the Renaissance to the modern day, offered a "facts and documents" approach that complemented Neher's more essayistic style.[7] Her specific research into the Balfour Declaration and the entry of Jews into French society (1750–1850) remains foundational for understanding the "Israelite" identity that Neher sought to reform.[7]
Legacy: Rebuilding the Jewish Soul
André Neher died in 1988, but his influence continues to be felt in both the Francophone and Israeli worlds. He transformed the image of the "French Jew" from a purely secular citizen of "the religion of the state" into a "Hebrew man"—a man of origins and prophetic vocation.[8]
The Van Leer Institute and Contemporary Impact
In Israel, the Van Leer Jerusalem Institute has led the effort to critique and disseminate his work.[26, 30] Recent scholarship has noted that Neher’s philosophy of the "middle" remains a vital alternative to the increasing polarization of Israeli society between "religious" and "secular" camps.[3, 26] His insistence that the Jewish challenge is to experience "everything together"—the old and the new, the holy and the profane—offers a dialectical model for a pluralistic Jewish identity.[3]
Furthermore, Neher’s investigation into the "silence of God" remains one of the most intellectually honest responses to the Holocaust in modern Jewish thought. By refusing to "explain away" the silence, and instead making silence the very ground of human freedom and responsibility, he provided a way for faith to survive in a world where the "Voice" often seems withdrawn.[2, 5, 19] His work reminds the modern reader that the "Exile of the Word" is not the end of the story, but the beginning of the "Prophetic Existence," where man is called to speak even when God is silent.[2, 5]
Conclusion: The Suspension Bridge of the Word
The lifework of André Neher can be summarized as a heroic attempt to maintain the "Word" in a century of silence. From his early days in Mahanaim to his final years in Jerusalem, he remained a "student of Abraham," constantly engaged in a "daring dialogue" with both God and humanity.[3, 5] He taught that the Jewish condition is one of permanent "ontological insecurity," yet it is precisely this insecurity that makes genuine freedom and ethical action possible.[2] His synthesis of the Maharal’s dialectics, the prophets’ existential call, and the harsh reality of the Shoah created a "Prophetic Humanism" that continues to offer profound insights into the nature of faith, language, and historical memory. In the "middle" space between the sacred and the profane, André Neher found not a compromise, but an "adventure of truth" that remains a beacon for post-Holocaust Jewish thought.[4, 23]

title: A Dialogue Between Silence and Prophecy: The Work, Torah and Philosophical Teaching, and Legacy of André Neher
source_file: דיאלוג בין השתיקה לנבואה- פועלו, משנתו התורנית וההגותית ומורשתו של אנדרה נהר.docx
content:
A Dialogue Between Silence and Prophecy: The Work, Torah and Philosophical Teaching, and Legacy of André Neher
Introduction: The Spiritual Portrait and Development of the Thinker of the Covenant and of Silence
Professor André Neher (1914–1988) was one of the most central, original and influential figures at the philosophical and intellectual crossroads of twentieth-century Judaism [cite: 1, 2]. Neher worked in the bilingual and bicultural space of France and Israel, and in his personality and writing he joined poles that often seemed irreconcilable [cite: 1]. He was a meticulous academic scholar who directed a university chair of the highest standing, and at the same time an existential thinker and a poet of the written word [cite: 1, 2]. He was a man rooted in the depths of the world of Jewish tradition and halakha, yet at the same time a committed humanist and universalist [cite: 1]. His thought was marked by a deep messianic vision of Hebrew history, interwoven with a pragmatic and sober political outlook [cite: 1].
Neher was born in 1914 in the town of Obernai (Obernai) in the Alsace region, and grew up within an Alsatian Jewish tradition that sought to combine fidelity to the commandments with deep involvement in European culture [cite: 2, 3]. He completed his secondary and academic studies at the Collège Freppel in Obernai, then at the Lycée Fustel de Coulanges and the University of Strasbourg, and qualified to teach German language and literature [cite: 2, 3]. The outbreak of the Second World War and the Nazi occupation cut short the course his life had been set to follow [cite: 2, 3]. Neher was forced to go into hiding with his family (his father Albert and his brother, the jurist Richard Neher) in the town of Brive-la-Gaillarde (Brive-la-Gaillarde), where he became part of the local Jewish community headed by Rabbi David Feuerwerker [cite: 2, 3].
For Neher, the years of persecution and existential danger became a period of intensive Torah study and searching philosophical inquiry [cite: 2]. Out of this contemplation of the physical and spiritual destruction of European Jewry grew his first joint work with his brother, Transcendance et immanence ("Transcendence and Immanence", 1946), which laid the foundation for his future teaching [cite: 2, 3]. After the liberation of France, Neher was appointed in 1948 head of the chair of Jewish Studies at the University of Strasbourg, an institution where he taught for two decades and which he turned into a cultural and spiritual center combining academic research with Jewish renewal [cite: 2, 3].
At the center of Neher's philosophy stands the concept of "the Covenant" (L'Alliance) that binds together God, man and God's people, the people of Israel [cite: 2]. He does not conceive of the Covenant as a static legal contract or a dogmatic obligation, but as an existential and dynamic drama of dialogue, freedom, responsibility and listening [cite: 1, 2, 4]. From this conception Neher examined the phenomenon of prophecy, the silence of God in catastrophe, and the meaning of the Return to Zion in the generation after the Holocaust [cite: 1, 4, 5].
The Paris School of Jewish Thought and the Transformation of French Jewry after the Holocaust
The physical and spiritual destruction wrought by the Holocaust confronted the Jewish intellectuals of France with an existential need to rebuild their cultural identity [cite: 6, 7]. The classic French emancipatory model, which advocated cultural assimilation and the relegation of Judaism to the private sphere alone, collapsed in the face of modern antisemitism and the extermination of European Jewry [cite: 7]. Against this background arose the "Paris School of Jewish Thought" (L'École de pensée juive de Paris), founded around educational institutions such as the teachers' college at Orsay (École d'Orsay) and consolidated in the annual gatherings of the "Colloquium of French-Speaking Jewish Intellectuals" (Colloque des intellectuels juifs de langue française) [cite: 7, 8, 9, 10]. This school, guided by key figures such as Jacob Gordin, sought to create a new synthesis between the worlds of Western thought and the classical Jewish sources [cite: 7, 10].
The spiritual and intellectual leadership of the Paris School rested on an exceptional philosophical trio, each of whose members represented a unique and fundamental dimension of Jewish thought and gave regular lectures at these gatherings [cite: 1, 6, 7]:
The philosopher Emmanuel Levinas translated Talmudic thought into a phenomenological-existential language, and presented Judaism as the root of universal ethics and of man's responsibility toward the other [cite: 1, 6, 7]. Rabbi Yehuda Léon Askénazi ("Manitou") presented the esoteric teaching, Kabbalah and messianic historiosophy, emphasizing the transition from a passive exilic identity to a Hebrew national identity realized in the Land of Israel [cite: 1, 6, 7]. André Neher was entrusted with the field of the Bible and prophecy, and brought into intellectual discourse the dramatic, literary and existential language of the Hebrew Bible [cite: 1, 6].
This division of roles reflected a complex historiosophical conception: the Talmud provided the normative and ethical structure, the Kabbalah provided the metaphysical and messianic dimension, and the Bible supplied the existential, dialogical and historical root [cite: 1, 6]. The combination of the three created a cultural movement that refused to apologize for its religious and national identity [cite: 6, 7]. Within this framework the school re-examined fundamental concepts of the French Republic; thus, for example, the concept of "fraternity" (Fraternité) was analyzed by Neher and Manitou through a reading of the deeds of the Patriarchs in the Book of Genesis [cite: 6, 11]. Neher showed how the drama of Cain and Abel represents the existential challenge of the relation to the other, in which fraternity is not a natural given but a moral demand accompanied by the danger of violence and rivalry [cite: 6, 11].
Alongside his intellectual activity in Paris, Neher turned Strasbourg into a center of absorption and integration for the Jews of North Africa (and especially those from Algeria) who arrived in France in the 1950s and 1960s [cite: 2]. Neher saw their arrival as a vital layer in the physical and spiritual renewal of the community, and worked with Catholic and Protestant leaders to secure recognition of the rights of the Jews and of their national and Zionist identity [cite: 2].
His Biblical Teaching and Theory of Prophecy: A Canonical-Existential Reading
Most of Neher's scholarly and philosophical work is devoted to the analysis of the biblical text and to deciphering the phenomenon of prophecy. In the series of his principal works, Amos, contribution à l'étude du prophétisme ("Amos: A Contribution to the Study of Prophecy", 1950), L'Essence du prophétisme ("The Essence of Prophecy", 1955), Moïse et la vocation juive ("Moses and the Jewish Vocation", 1956) and Jérémie ("Jeremiah", 1960), Neher developed a unique interpretive methodology that places him beyond the traditional struggle between religious dogmatism and critical-scholarly biblical criticism [cite: 1, 2, 3, 12].
Neher had a thorough knowledge of the philological and historical rules of academic research, but refrained from using the methods of German-Protestant biblical criticism [cite: 1]. He argued that this school, led by scholars such as Julius Wellhausen, grew out of Christian theological presuppositions that sought to break the biblical text up into different sources and to separate an early "moral prophecy" from a late "legal priesthood" [cite: 1].
Instead, Neher advocated a "canonical reading" (Lecture canonique), which grasps the biblical text as it lies before us as a coherent and complete whole [cite: 1]. He explained that the difficulties, duplications and contradictions in the text are not evidence of the joining together of different sources, but deliberate expressions of the existential complexity and the inner dialectic of the encounter between the divine and the human [cite: 1].
The application of this methodology is prominent in his book on the prophet Amos, in which Neher grappled with the argumentative contradiction between verses that stress Israel's exclusive election and verses that present Israel as equal in worth to all the nations [cite: 1]. Neher showed that both of these aspects rest on the concept of "the Covenant", which contains at one and the same time a particular aspect (the unique covenant with the people of Israel) and a universal aspect (the covenant with the descendants of Noah and with all humanity) [cite: 1]. The contradiction is not a textual failure, but a reflection of the constant tension in which the Jewish people lives between its particular vocation and its responsibility to all humankind [cite: 1].
Neher's conception of prophecy places the prophet at the center of a turbulent existential drama. The prophet is not passive, nor a soothsayer who captures visions, but a figure acting within an existential tension between the freedom of God and the freedom of man [cite: 1]. Prophecy is an encounter in which God turns to man and asks him to be a partner in history [cite: 1, 2]. The prophet is required to bear the heavy burden of the divine word before a recalcitrant society, often taking a stand as a fierce defender against the divine judgment in order to protect his people [cite: 1].
"The Exile of the Word" and the Silence of God: From the Bible to Auschwitz
Neher's most famous and influential work in the field of the philosophy of religion is L'Exil de la Parole. Du silence biblique au silence d'Auschwitz ("The Exile of the Word: From the Silence of the Bible to the Silence of Auschwitz", 1970) [cite: 3, 5, 13]. In this book Neher formulated a searching existential theology for the reality after the Holocaust, and placed himself at the heart of the international philosophical discourse concerned with the modern crisis of faith [cite: 4, 5, 14].
Neher's central question does not concern the human evil revealed in the Holocaust, but "the silence of God": the metaphysical scandal of a God who does not intervene in history in a time of catastrophe [cite: 4, 15]. Neher rejects the classical theodicean attempts to explain the Holocaust as punishment for sins or as a trial, and argues that silence is not total absence or lack, but a fundamental ontological and dialogical category in the Bible and in Jewish existence [cite: 4, 16, 17].
Neher analyzes the occurrences of silence in the biblical text and shows that the divine-human dialogue consists not only of words but also of stillness [cite: 4, 5]. Abraham walks to Mount Moriah at the Binding of Isaac amid absolute divine silence, and Job cries out from his suffering before a God who does not answer [cite: 14, 18]. This biblical silence is the space in which human freedom and pure faith are tested, a faith that is not conditional on reward or on an immediate answer [cite: 4].
In a bold parallel, Neher presents the silence of Auschwitz as the extreme continuation of biblical silence [cite: 4, 5, 17]. Auschwitz represents "the exile of the word": a state in which the divine word and the human word have been sealed off [cite: 4, 5, 17]. Against philosophical conceptions that see being as a dichotomous division between "being" and "nothingness", Neher formulates a Jewish ontology based on the category of "perhaps" (Peut-Être) [cite: 4, 17, 19]. The "perhaps" is the space of possibility, of messianic expectation and of a hope that does not surrender to despair [cite: 4, 17, 19].
Jewish faith after the Holocaust, according to Neher, is not based on theological certainty or on consoling wholeness, but on "hope against all hope" (Espérance contre tout espoir) [cite: 4, 17, 19]. This faith is anchored in the willingness to live within risk, tears and silence, and to continue the struggle for life and the building of history anew [cite: 3, 4, 17].
The Jewish Renaissance and Modernity: The Maharal of Prague, David Gans and Science
Alongside his biblical studies, Neher devoted a series of in-depth historical-philosophical studies to rabbinic thought in the 16th century, and in particular to the school of the Maharal of Prague (Rabbi Yehuda Loew ben Bezalel). His outstanding works in this field include Le Puits de l'Exil ("The Well of Exile: The Dialectical Theology of the Maharal of Prague", 1966), David Gans, 1541-1613 (1974), and Faust et le Maharal de Prague ("Faust and the Maharal of Prague: Myth and Reality", 1987) [cite: 3, 12, 13].
These studies included a historiographical and philosophical revision of the standing of the Maharal [cite: 1]. Scholars of Jewish Studies, such as Jacob Katz and Rivka Schatz-Uffenheimer, saw the Maharal as a conservative, anti-humanist and insular thinker who set an abyss between Israel and the nations and rejected the secular sciences [cite: 1]. Neher came out forcefully against this view, and showed that the Maharal's teaching contains a complex dialectical theology [cite: 1, 3]. In his view, the Maharal did not fight against science or humanism, but offered a broad theognostic humanism in which every nation and every creature has an organic place in the cosmic order [cite: 1]. The Maharal recognized the lawfulness of nature and the value of science, but demanded that they be integrated within an all-embracing metaphysical consciousness [cite: 1].
In his study of David Gans, a disciple of the Maharal and of the Rema, who worked as an assistant to the astronomers Tycho Brahe and Johannes Kepler, Neher uncovered a chapter in the encounter between rabbinic thought and the scientific revolution of the Renaissance [cite: 3, 12]. Neher showed how a deeply rooted religious thinker could be an active partner in the breakthrough of modern astronomy, creating a synthesis between monotheistic faith and scientific modernity [cite: 3, 12].
In his late work Neher compared the Faust myth with the legend of the Maharal's Golem [cite: 3, 12, 13]. Neher showed that while the European Faustian model represents a human hubris that strives for unlimited control and leads to self-destruction and a pact with the devil, the Maharal's Golem represents a creation bounded by halakha and morality, whose purpose is the protection of life and the repair of the world [cite: 3, 12, 13].

Immigration to Jerusalem, Reception in Academia and Public Legacy
In 1974, at the age of 60 and with the peak of his professional fame in France behind him, André Neher realized his Zionist vision and immigrated to Israel together with his wife, the historian Renée Neher-Bernheim [cite: 2, 3]. The couple made their home in Jerusalem, where Neher lived and worked until his death in 1988 [cite: 1, 3]. For him, immigration to Jerusalem was not merely a personal or geographical step, but the existential realization of his messianic conception: an active response to the historical events of the reunification of Jerusalem and the Six-Day War, in which he saw a turning point in the covenant between the people, the land and God [cite: 1, 18].
Despite his standing as the most senior thinker of French Jewry, Neher's reception in the academic and cultural establishment in Israel was fraught with difficulties, disappointments and marginalization [cite: 1]. The main difficulty stemmed from a sharp methodological and generic gap [cite: 1]. The principal genre in which Neher wrote was the philosophical-literary essay (Essai), characterized by personal, poetic and fluent writing, with few footnotes and dry philological discussions [cite: 1].
By contrast, Jewish Studies in Israel at that time, led by the positivist school of the Hebrew University, demanded rigorous philological-historical research and strict reliance on texts [cite: 1]. The academic establishment in Israel restricted Neher's steps and accused him of resolving textual and scholarly difficulties in the Bible and in Renaissance thought by means of metaphysical, ideological and religious presuppositions [cite: 1].
Neher's rejection by the academic establishment placed him alongside other eminent thinkers whom Israeli academia found hard to digest because of their philosophical and non-disciplinary writing, such as Martin Buber and Abraham Joshua Heschel [cite: 1]. Neher himself strengthened this intellectual affinity and regarded himself as a disciple of Heschel [cite: 1]. Because of these difficulties, Neher was not fully absorbed into the Hebrew University, but divided his time between academic activity at Tel Aviv University and teaching in Strasbourg, and his extensive thought remained to a large extent hidden and unknown to the Hebrew reading public [cite: 1, 2, 21].
In the political sphere, too, Neher was sometimes perceived as a naive metaphysician, but his positions were pragmatic and complex [cite: 1]. Neher opposed a utopian messianism that ascribes absolute sanctity to the institutions of the state or to territory, and stressed that the state is a historical instrument in the struggle for existence [cite: 1]. He firmly opposed religious coercion and a coercive Orthodox establishmentarianism, and welcomed the secular and democratic aspects of the State of Israel, while maintaining a critical tension between Jewish identity and Israeli identity [cite: 1].
The legacy of André Neher offers a unique bridge between the silence of catastrophe and the prophetic word, and between the depth of tradition and humanist culture [cite: 1, 4, 5]. His conception of the canonical reading of the Bible, the ontology of the "perhaps", and the constant dialogue within the divine-human covenant continue to serve as a central source of inspiration for modern Jewish research and thought [cite: 1, 2, 4].
